units.title: Hit the nail on the head
units.grammar_focus: High-frequency conversational idioms (hit the nail on the head, break the ice, read between the lines, the elephant in the room, the tip of the iceberg)
units.real_life_context: You react to ideas, observations, and conversations with idioms that signal genuine engagement.

grammar.sentence: When she said the team was burned out, she _____.
options: hit the nail on the head
hit the nail on the floor
grammar.answer: hit the nail on the head
grammar.explanation: "Hit the nail on the head" = identify exactly the right point or cause. Fixed idiom — no substitutions. The image is of striking a nail squarely, not glancing off. Used to validate someone else's precise observation.

grammar.sentence: Someone has to address _____ — we can't keep avoiding it.
grammar.explanation: "The elephant in the room" = a large, obvious problem everyone is ignoring. Fixed prepositional structure "in the room". Used to introduce something that needs saying but hasn't been.

grammar.sentence: She didn't say it directly, but if you _____ the lines, the answer is no.
grammar.explanation: "Read between the lines" = infer meaning not explicitly stated. Used when someone communicates indirectly and you've decoded the real message. Crucial idiom for navigating polite refusals.

grammar.sentence: What we know is just the tip of iceberg — the real problem is much bigger.
grammar.answer: What we know is just the tip of the iceberg — the real problem is much bigger.
grammar.explanation: "The tip of the iceberg" — definite article "the" is part of the fixed idiom. The image: only 10% of an iceberg shows above water; the rest is submerged. Used to indicate a small visible part of a much larger hidden whole.

grammar.passage: The consultant's first report was diplomatic but unmistakable. 'You've hit the nail on the head on customer churn, but that's only the tip of the iceberg. The real elephant in the room is the leadership culture — and reading between the lines of your own employee survey, your people already know it.'
grammar.question: According to the consultant, what is the bigger issue beneath customer churn?
grammar.answer: the leadership culture (or "the elephant in the room — leadership culture")
grammar.explanation: Four C1 idioms stacked: "hit the nail on the head" (precise diagnosis), "the tip of the iceberg" (visible portion), "the elephant in the room" (avoided real problem), "reading between the lines" (decoding implicit messages). Consulting-grade prose.

listening_speaking.text: You hit the nail on the head.

We need to break the ice somehow.

units.title: Bite the bullet, cold feet
units.grammar_focus: Body and emotion idioms (bite the bullet, get cold feet, pull someone's leg, cost an arm and a leg, head over heels)
units.real_life_context: You describe decisions, hesitations, and emotional states with idiomatic precision.

grammar.sentence: I'm going to _____ and tell her tomorrow.
grammar.explanation: "Bite the bullet" = force yourself to do something unpleasant or difficult. Fixed singular "the bullet". Origin: 19th-century battlefield surgery without anaesthesia — soldiers literally bit bullets to endure pain. Now used metaphorically for any unwelcome but necessary action.

grammar.sentence: He got _____ at the altar and called it off.
grammar.explanation: "Get cold feet" = lose nerve at the last moment, typically before a big commitment. Always plural "feet". The image is of feet literally going cold from fear, freezing you in place. Common in wedding/career/decision contexts.

grammar.sentence: Stop joking — are you _____ my leg?
grammar.explanation: "Pull someone's leg" = tease or joke with someone, usually with a deliberately untrue statement they might believe. Used informally to check whether a claim is serious. Origin disputed but likely 19th-century British.

grammar.sentence: The repair costed an arm and the leg.
grammar.hint: Use "cost" (past = "cost") and "an arm and a leg"
grammar.answer: The repair cost an arm and a leg.
grammar.explanation: Two corrections: "cost" is irregular (cost / cost / cost — no "costed"), and the idiom is "an arm and a leg" with article "a" twice. Both elements common at C1 — first as conjugation, second as fixed idiom form.

grammar.passage: She had been engaged for three months when she finally bit the bullet and admitted she was getting cold feet. Her sister, who never pulled her leg about anything serious, told her plainly: 'A wedding costs an arm and a leg. Calling it off costs less than staying in.'
grammar.question: Which idiom in the passage means "to hesitate at the last moment"?
grammar.explanation: "Cold feet" = hesitação de última hora, especialmente antes de um compromisso grande (casamento, decisão). Outros idioms no texto: "bit the bullet" (forçar-se), "pulled her leg" (provocar), "costs an arm and a leg" (caríssimo).

listening_speaking.text: I'll just bite the bullet and tell her.

units.title: Piece of cake, spill the beans
units.grammar_focus: Food idioms and difficulty/secret idioms (a piece of cake, spill the beans, take with a grain of salt, a tough nut to crack, that's the way the cookie crumbles)
units.real_life_context: You describe ease, difficulty, secrets, and acceptance using everyday food-based idioms.

grammar.sentence: The interview was _____ — over in fifteen minutes.
grammar.explanation: "A piece of cake" = very easy. Fixed article "a", not "the". Used to describe tasks that turned out simpler than feared. Origin: cake was associated with simple pleasures or as a prize for easy contests.

grammar.sentence: Don't _____ the beans before the announcement is official.
grammar.explanation: "Spill the beans" = reveal a secret, often prematurely or accidentally. Fixed verb "spill" + "the beans". Origin disputed (possibly ancient Greek voting with beans). Modern usage: any premature disclosure.

grammar.sentence: Take what he says with a _____ of salt — he exaggerates.
grammar.explanation: "Take with a grain of salt" = treat with healthy scepticism. British variant: "pinch of salt". The image: a small dose of salt was once thought to neutralise poisons; metaphorically, a small dose of doubt neutralises misleading claims.

grammar.sentence: She's a hard nut to broke.
grammar.answer: She's a tough nut to crack.
accepts: She's a hard nut to crack.
grammar.explanation: "Crack" is the fixed verb in this idiom — you "crack" a nut, not "break" it (although physically you do break shells, the idiom is fixed). "Tough" or "hard" both work, but the verb is non-negotiable.

grammar.passage: She had assumed the conversation would be a piece of cake — a quick update, no drama. Then he spilled the beans about the merger, told her to take half of what corporate said with a grain of salt, and warned her that the head of legal was a tough nut to crack. 'That's the way the cookie crumbles,' he said, smiling weakly.
grammar.question: How did he describe the head of legal?
grammar.explanation: Five food idioms packed into one passage: "a piece of cake" (easy), "spilled the beans" (revealed secret), "with a grain of salt" (sceptically), "a tough nut to crack" (hard person/problem), "the way the cookie crumbles" (acceptance of bad luck). Food idioms cluster naturally.

listening_speaking.text: The exam was a piece of cake.
Don't spill the beans yet.
Take that report with a grain of salt.
He's a tough nut to crack.
That's the way the cookie crumbles.

units.title: Two birds with one stone
units.grammar_focus: Animal idioms and efficiency/strategy idioms (kill two birds with one stone, the ball is in your court, burn bridges, play it by ear, a wild goose chase, on the same page)
units.real_life_context: You describe strategy, position, and approach with animal and game-based idioms.

grammar.sentence: If we combine the meetings, we _____ with one stone.
grammar.explanation: "Kill two birds with one stone" = accomplish two goals with one action. Fixed numbers — "two birds", "one stone". Used heavily in business and planning contexts. Modern alternatives: "feed two birds with one scone" (cruelty-free version, used jokingly).

grammar.sentence: The proposal is on her desk now — _____ is in her court.
grammar.explanation: "The ball is in your court" = it's your turn to act or decide. Tennis/court image — the ball has been passed across. Used to signal that the speaker has done their part and now the other party must respond.

grammar.sentence: We don't have a fixed schedule for the weekend — we'll just play it _____.
grammar.explanation: "Play it by ear" = improvise, decide as you go, without a fixed plan. Origin: musicians playing without sheet music, by hearing. Now used for any flexible approach to plans.

grammar.sentence: Don't burn the bridges with that company — you might need them later.
grammar.answer: Don't burn bridges with that company — you might need them later.
grammar.explanation: "Burn bridges" = sever a relationship permanently in a way that prevents return. Idiom uses plural "bridges" without article. The image: armies historically burned bridges behind them to prevent retreat or pursuit. Modern usage: relational/professional contexts.

grammar.passage: She had spent six weeks chasing a contract that her boss called 'a wild goose chase from the start.' But she had managed to kill two birds with one stone — the meetings had revealed an entirely different opportunity, and she and the new prospect were now firmly on the same page. The ball was in legal's court, and she was content to play the rest of it by ear.
grammar.question: According to the passage, what does she plan to do about the rest of the deal?
accepts: play the rest of it by ear
grammar.explanation: Five idioms in one paragraph: "a wild goose chase" (fruitless pursuit), "kill two birds with one stone" (dual gain), "on the same page" (in agreement), "the ball is in legal's court" (their move), "play it by ear" (improvise). Strategic-speak at C1.

units.title: Crystal clear, low-hanging fruit
units.grammar_focus: Compound idioms, similes, and modern business metaphors (crystal clear, low-hanging fruit, moving target, double-edged sword, like watching paint dry, a blessing in disguise)
units.real_life_context: You diversify your figurative range — using similes ("as X as Y" / "like + clause") and modern business metaphors alongside classical idioms.

grammar.sentence: Her instructions were _____ — no room for misinterpretation.
grammar.explanation: "Crystal clear" — compound adjective meaning perfectly transparent or unambiguous. Fixed form. Image: a flawless crystal lets all light through. Now used metaphorically for any communication that leaves no doubt.

grammar.sentence: Let's start with the _____ — the easy wins first.
grammar.explanation: "Low-hanging fruit" — easy gains that require little effort. Fixed hyphenation, singular use. Common in strategy and consulting. Origin: orchards — pick the fruit you can reach first. Mass-noun usage: "the low-hanging fruit", not "fruits".

grammar.sentence: Working from home is a _____ sword — flexible but isolating.
grammar.explanation: "A double-edged sword" — something with both positive and negative consequences. Fixed compound adjective "double-edged". The image: a sword sharp on both sides cuts in two directions.

grammar.sentence: The conference was like to watch paint dry.
grammar.answer: The conference was like watching paint dry.
grammar.explanation: Simile pattern: "like + -ing form" or "like + noun phrase". Never "like + to-infinitive". "Like watching paint dry" = extremely boring. Common simile to express boredom vividly.

grammar.passage: The reorg was, in retrospect, a blessing in disguise. The strategy memo had been crystal clear, even if the timing was a moving target. We picked off the low-hanging fruit in the first month and learned that scaling, for us, was a double-edged sword. Without the disruption, we would have spent another year doing what felt like watching paint dry.
grammar.question: How does the speaker describe scaling?
grammar.explanation: Six figurative expressions: "a blessing in disguise" (hidden gift), "crystal clear" (transparent), "a moving target" (constantly shifting), "low-hanging fruit" (easy wins), "a double-edged sword" (mixed blessing), "like watching paint dry" (boredom simile). Strategy memo prose at C1.

cross_unit_consolidation: Use high-frequency conversational idioms in fitting contexts (hit the nail on the head, the elephant in the room, the tip of the iceberg, read between the lines, break the ice)
Deploy body and emotion idioms (bite the bullet, get cold feet, pull someone's leg, cost an arm and a leg)
Use food idioms (a piece of cake, spill the beans, take with a grain of salt, a tough nut to crack)
Apply animal/strategy idioms (kill two birds with one stone, the ball is in your court, burn bridges, play it by ear, on the same page)
Layer modern business metaphors (crystal clear, low-hanging fruit, a moving target, a double-edged sword, a blessing in disguise)
Form similes correctly: "like + -ing form" or "like + noun phrase", never "like + to-infinitive"
Avoid mixing metaphors within one clause
